title: B+ tree
text: A B-tree can store keys in internal nodes. A B+ tree does not. OntoDB uses the B+ tree shape because a SPARQL range is a walk along sibling leaves, and that walk should not climb back to the root for every key. The key is a TripleKey , 24 bytes. The value in a leaf is the key itself: the triple is the record. There is no separate tuple id. Every page is 4096 bytes. The first 8 bytes are the pageLSN, little-endian. Payload starts at offset 8. A stored LSN of 0 means unset. INVALID_LSN is -1. Page layout The byte layout is written in the page headers. After the 8-byte pageLSN, every index page has a 12-byte header: type, size, and max size, each a 4-byte integer in the machine's byte order. A leaf follows with its right sibling's page id and an array of 24-byte keys: 169 per page. An internal page follows with slots of a 24-byte key and a 4-byte child id: 145 slots, so 144 keys. Keys are stored whole, with no prefix compression. The header page keeps the root id just after the pageLSN. The contracts: An internal page stores n keys and n + 1 children. KeyAt(0) is unused. ValueAt(0) is the leftmost child. A leaf stores keys in increasing order and a right-sibling page id. MaxSize() is at least 2, and the page fits in PAGE_SIZE . The header page stores the root, or INVALID_PAGE_ID when the tree is empty. GetLSN / SetLSN are the page's pageLSN. A zeroed page is not a valid header until the root is initialized to INVALID_PAGE_ID . Planned Plans 2.1 to 2.7 are done; scripts/check index runs them all. The tree is single-threaded until crabbing (plan 7.1). Order CheckInvariants returns nullopt when the tree is well formed, otherwise a description of the first broken rule. Check size, order, sibling links, and the separator rule: keys in child i - 1 are strictly less than KeyAt(i) , and keys in child i are greater than or equal to it. CheckInvariants also checks the minimum fill (every node but the root at least half its maximum), that every leaf is at the same depth, and that each key lies in the range its ancestors' separators allow. It reads one page at a time, so it runs on a tiny pool. ToString prints one line per level. ToDot is a Graphviz digraph, with dashed edges for sibling links. \tree spo and \tree spo dot call these on the indexed backend; with the memory backend they answer no index , and an index the store does not have answers no index named ... . Point search GetValue walks from the root to a leaf. An empty tree is empty. A missing key returns false. The pinned-frame count is zero on return. The header page must be created with Init , which stores INVALID_PAGE_ID ; a zeroed header would read as a tree rooted at page 0. Insert and split A duplicate insert returns false. A full leaf splits. A full internal page splits, including the split that creates a new root. Separators stay consistent with the leaves. Pick copy-up or copy-down and test the parent separator against the leaf. If you copy the middle key up and also leave it in the left leaf, the separator rule fails: the right leaf's first key is not strictly greater than a separator that still sits in the left leaf. After the pages agree, call: CrashPoint::Reach("BPlusTree::Insert::after_leaf_split") CrashPoint::Reach("BPlusTree::Insert::after_internal_split") — a root split counts Unpin before returning. The random-insert test compares the tree to a sorted std::vector . OntoDB splits in the middle: a leaf keeps the left half and copies the right half's first key up; an internal page moves its middle key up. Pages store no parent pointer. An insert remembers the page ids on its way down, releasing each page before reading its child, and re-fetches a parent by id only if the split reaches it. That keeps at most three pages pinned and is correct while one thread changes the tree. The constructor takes optional maximum node sizes, defaulting to what a page holds. Tests pass sizes as small as 2 to grow deep trees from few keys; a randomized test checks every invariant after

title: Buffer pool
text: PAGE_SIZE is 4096. Every page image, including ones written before any log exists, reserves 8 bytes at offset 0 for the pageLSN. The rest is payload. That reservation is why logging can be added later without reformatting the file. Disk manager DiskManager owns the database file. AllocatePage ids are stable across restart. ReadPage and WritePage move exactly one page, including the pageLSN. A page never written reads back as zeros. ShutDown flushes and closes. When stats are installed, count PageRead and PageWrite . Trace component "disk" . Write the bytes you were given. Do not invent a second header in front of the page. The file's length is the allocation record. AllocatePage grows the file by one zero page, so a restart sees every page allocated before it, and page 0 is an ordinary page (the catalog uses it). DeallocatePage does not reuse the id: the file only grows, because a reused id that a log record still names would send redo into someone else's page. WritePage goes through the page cache and does not fsync ; ShutDown does, and a failed fsync throws instead of retrying. A write past the end grows the file, and a read past the end returns zeros, so recovery can redo a record for a page the file has not reached yet. A negative page id, or any call after ShutDown , throws StorageException . Planned Plan 1.1 is done. scripts/check 1.1 . Disk scheduler One background thread drains a queue of DiskRequest . Schedule returns immediately. The promise is set when the I/O finishes, on the scheduler thread, not the caller. The destructor finishes queued work and joins. The caller's buffer stays valid until then. Trace component "io" . The query thread must not call ReadPage itself once the scheduler exists. A prefetch and a flush can then overlap the CPU work. The promise is moved into the queue. Do not touch it after Schedule . Requests run in the order they were scheduled, so a write followed by a read of the same page reads what was written. If the disk manager throws, the exception is stored in the promise and get() rethrows it. Plan 1.2 is done; scripts/check 1.2 . LRU-K RecordAccess appends a timestamp. A frame with fewer than k accesses has infinite backward k-distance. Evict picks the evictable frame with the largest distance, and breaks ties by the older k-th access. It returns false when nothing is evictable, and it does not write frame_id . SetEvictable(false) keeps history so a page that is pinned and unpinned does not look new. Remove drops history. Size is the evictable count. The replacer is thread-safe. Trace component "replacer" . Infinite distance is larger than every finite distance. A frame touched once is thrown out before a frame touched k times. The default k in the shell is 2. \set lru_k K stores the knob. The pool has to be built with that k for it to matter. The classic paper is O'Neil, O'Neil, and Weikum, "The LRU-K Page Replacement Algorithm". k = 1 is LRU. Time is a logical clock that ticks on every RecordAccess , so eviction is deterministic. Among frames with infinite distance, the one whose oldest recorded access is earliest goes first; with k = 2 that is LRU among frames seen once. Evict drops the victim's history. A frame id out of range throws std::invalid_argument . Choosing a victim scans every frame, which is cheap at the default 64. Plan 1.3 is done; scripts/check 1.3 . Buffer pool Thread-safe from the first version. NewPage allocates, pins, and returns a zeroed frame. FetchPage pins, and reads from disk on a miss. UnpinPage drops one pin and marks dirty when asked. DeletePage fails when the page is pinned. GetPinnedFrameCount is safe to call from a test thread while a query runs. BufferHit on a memory fetch, BufferMiss when a frame is read from disk. Trace component "bpm" . One latch covers the page table, the free list, pins, dirty bits, and the replacer, and it is held across the disk read of a miss or the write-back of a victim. Every read and write goes through the scheduler. When a lo

title: Code design
text: Patterns Pattern Where Iterator (volcano) TripleIterator ; every executor's Init / Next pulls one row at a time Repository TripleStore and Dictionary hide where triples and terms live ( MemStore , IndexedStore ; MemDictionary , DiskDictionary ) Factory ExecutorFactory::Create maps a plan node to its executor; Database::Open ; the LogRecord named constructors; MakeDamagePolicy Builder Planner builds the plan tree from a bound query Strategy, replace conditional with polymorphism LogDamagePolicy , one class per recovery mode ; \set join selects the join operator; TraceSink implementations Null object NullTraceSink when tracing is off Decorator RecordingStore wraps any TripleStore and records its changes, so a statement can be logged as one transaction or undone Adapter RdfLoader adapts raptor2's parser to Dictionary and TripleStore Command The shell's command table, one entry per backslash command, read by both dispatch and \help ; log records are replayable commands RAII ReadPageGuard and WritePageGuard unpin on destruction Dependency injection ExecutorContext carries the store, dictionary, config, and stats into every executor; LogManager , Durability , and the buffer pool take their collaborators as constructor arguments Adding to OntoDB To add Where A shell command One entry in tools/shell/commands.cpp : word, usage, summary, handler. \help picks it up An executor A class with Init / Next , a plan node, and a case in ExecutorFactory::Create A storage backend A TripleStore implementation; the engine sees only the interface A recovery mode A LogDamagePolicy subclass and a case in MakeDamagePolicy A verify check A function returning a CheckResult (ok, report line), added to Durability::Verify Deliberate exceptions No retry on a failed fsync. A log flush that fails is reported, not retried. After a failed fsync the kernel may already have dropped the dirty pages, so a retry that succeeds can still have lost data; this is the lesson of PostgreSQL's 2018 fsync incident. One process-wide test hook. CrashPoint is global because a crash point has to be reachable from any depth of any call. It does nothing unless a test arms it. Constants, not literals. Sizes and intervals have names: PAGE_SIZE and the defaults in common/config.h , LogRecord::kHeaderSize and kMaxSize , kFlushInterval in the log manager, and kDefaultLogTail in the shell. Further reading Gamma, Helm, Johnson, and Vlissides, *Design Patterns*. Fowler, *Refactoring*, on replacing conditionals with polymorphism and extracting functions.

title: Concurrency
text: The shell is autocommit unless you say \begin . \commit and \abort end the explicit transaction. \session N runs the following commands on worker N. A blocked session prints session 2 waiting: X lock held by txn 5 . Isolation is a setting: \set isolation ru|rc|rr|ser . The default in Config is read committed. The concurrency feature runs under ThreadSanitizer. scripts/check concurrency builds the tsan preset. Latches and locks A latch is held for a tree operation and is released before the operation returns. That protocol is crabbing . A lock is held for a transaction. Strict 2PL means an exclusive lock is held until commit or abort, at every isolation level, including read uncommitted. Releasing an exclusive lock early would let another transaction read or write a value this transaction might still abort. Lock modes Resources are the database, an index ( "spo" , "pos" , "osp" ), and a key. Take IS or IX on the database and on the index before S or X on a key. Grant order on one resource is FIFO. Mode Compatible with IS IS, IX, S, SIX IX IS, IX S IS, S SIX IS X nothing The same transaction may upgrade in place. An upgrade does not jump ahead of a waiter. Lock blocks until the request is granted or the transaction is aborted. Before blocking, if a session was passed in, call SetWaiting with the reason, and ClearWaiting when the wait ends. The waiting thread is the one inside Lock , so the reason has to be set before the wait. The shell polls it. Isolation The specs in test/isolation/specs/ are the contract. Twelve of them cover dirty read, nonrepeatable read, lost update, lock upgrade, two deadlocks, write-write conflict, abort releasing locks, and phantoms. Read uncommitted takes no shared locks. A dirty read is allowed. Read committed releases shared locks at the end of the statement. A value you read can change before you commit. You do not see uncommitted writes. Repeatable read holds shared locks until commit. A row you read stays. A row you did not read can appear. Serializable holds shared locks until commit and adds the phantom mechanism from plan 7.6. The mechanism is locks, not snapshots. MVCC is an open design with no stub. It is not a substitute you slip into the concurrency feature. A versioned reader is described with snapshots . Deadlock A background thread builds the waits-for graph and aborts the youngest transaction in each cycle. Younger means the larger id. The abort throws TransactionAbortException out of that transaction's Lock call. Aborting whoever happened to notice the cycle fails the spec: session 1 starts first, so it has the smaller id, and session 2 is the victim in both the two-key cycle and the upgrade cycle. Phantoms Repeatable read holds locks on triples you read. An insert of a new triple does not conflict with those locks, so a second scan can see Dana even though the first scan did not. The repeatable-read spec expects that. Do not "fix" it by taking a predicate lock at every isolation level. Serializable picks one extra mechanism: key-range locks, gap locks, or predicate locks. Write the choice in the header comment above the code. Under serializable the insert blocks until the reader commits. A predicate lock on ?s rdf:type ub:Student also blocks a transaction that inserts a course if your predicate is wider than the query. That cost is the reason to write down which predicate you actually locked. Transactions Begin returns a growing transaction. Ids increase from 1. Commit releases locks and moves to committed. Abort , when no log manager was installed, undoes the write set newest-first, releases locks, and moves to aborted. Newest-first matters: an insert followed by a delete of the same triple restores the wrong state if you undo the insert first. A committed or aborted transaction accepts no further work. The write set is temporary. Plan 8.4 replaces it with log undo when a LogManager was passed in. The constructor already takes that pointer so the signature does not change later. Null

title: Settings
text: Settings OntoDB> \set backend mem pool_size 64 lru_k 2 join nlj isolation rc Knob Values Default Effect today backend mem , indexed mem indexed moves the triples onto pages and B+ trees in a temporary file; mem moves them back. A persistent database stays on mem until PLAN 8 pool_size frames 64 Frames in the indexed backend's pool, read when the backend is switched on lru_k positive integer 2 The indexed backend's LRU-K k , read when the backend is switched on join auto , nlj , inlj , hash nlj Join operator, swapped into the plan before \explain and execution. auto keeps nested loop until the optimizer chooses (PLAN 5.4) isolation ru , rc , rr , ser rc Stored for transactions, which are being built A setting that is accepted prints ok . An unknown knob or value prints an error and changes nothing. Timing \timing on prints time: N ms after each statement's result. \timing off stops it. Statistics OntoDB> \stats page reads: 0 page writes: 0 buffer hits: 0 buffer misses: 0 log flushes: 0 log flushes counts physical log writes in a persistent database; one flush can carry many commits. The page and buffer counters stay at zero until the buffer pool exists.

title: Loading data
text: Formats Extension Format .ttl Turtle .nt N-Triples .rdf , .owl RDF/XML Parsing is done by raptor2. The load reports how many statements the file contains, including any already stored; a triple is stored once. OntoDB> \load data/pizza.ttl loaded 27 triples in 1.1 ms OWL An OWL ontology is stored as the RDF triples of its serialization: classes are rdf:type owl:Class triples, the hierarchy is rdfs:subClassOf triples, and restrictions are their blank-node structures. OntoDB does not reason, so nothing is inferred at load time. Persistent databases In a database opened with a directory, one \load is one transaction. Either every new triple of the file is committed, or, if the load fails, none is. The terms in the file are written to the log once, so ids stay the same after a restart. Sample data File Contents data/tiny.ttl A small university graph, 53 triples. The query ?s a ub:Student ; ub:name ?name returns Alice, Bob, and Cara data/tiny.owl A small materials ontology in RDF/XML, 14 triples data/pizza.ttl A small pizza ontology subset, 27 triples data/lubm/queries/ The 14 LUBM queries, with query 7 repaired so it parses Larger data sets scripts/fetch-data pizza # the full Pizza ontology into data/downloads/ scripts/fetch-data lubm # runs the LUBM generator (needs Java) for University0_0.owl data/downloads/ is not committed. Status The in-memory store compares every stored triple on insert, so loading a large file is slow. That is the in-memory store, not the format; the indexed store ( \set backend indexed ) and its bulk loader (PLAN 6.1) are what make large graphs fast.

title: Development
text: The plan PLAN.md in the repository is the feature list. Each feature is a group of slices with ids such as 1.4 or 8.6 . The ids appear in test names ( P8_6_... ) and in the shell's not built yet (PLAN x.y) messages. A test for an unbuilt slice is disabled; removing DISABLED_ is part of finishing the slice. Checks scripts/check durable # one feature: build, run its tests, print the next slice scripts/check 0.2 # one slice scripts/status # every slice, grouped by feature, and the progress scripts/crashtest --seeds 4 # the crash harness scripts/check configures and builds the right preset, runs the matching tests (including disabled ones, so you see what is left), and prints pass or fail and the next slice. Concurrency slices run under ThreadSanitizer. Continuous integration Every push builds and runs the whole test suite under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and again under ThreadSanitizer, then checks formatting with clang-format and lints src/ and tools/ with clang-tidy, warnings as errors. Test harnesses Harness What it checks Query harness ( test/queries/*.test ) SPARQL text and expected rows in canonical spelling, compared as a multiset unless order is declared Isolation harness ( test/isolation/specs/ ) A scripted schedule over two sessions, checking blocked , unblocks , abort , contains , equals , absent Crash harness ( scripts/crashtest ) Kills a child process at random points and compares the reopened store with a store that replayed only acknowledged commits Durability scenarios ( test/durable/ ) Load, update, crash before commit, crash during checkpoint, torn and corrupt logs, corrupt snapshot, verify, and a full shell session Crash points are named Class::Method::point and are armed by tests through CrashPoint::Arm . Code layout src/include/ headers, one directory per component src/ implementations, mirroring the headers tools/shell/ the ontodb shell test/ GoogleTest suites, mirroring src/ data/ sample ontologies and LUBM queries scripts/ check, status, crashtest, fetch-data benchmarks/ one directory per measured question writeups/ one file per finding

title: Dictionary
text: term_id_t is a uint64_t . Ids start at 1. INVALID_TERM_ID is the maximum uint64 and means unbound, not a term. No dictionary may assign it: Dictionary::CheckAssignable throws StorageException if the next id would be INVALID_TERM_ID . Rows rely on it to mark empty slots, and the triple key's saturated upper bound relies on no stored key containing it. Zero is not a valid id, so a zeroed key does not accidentally name the first term you interned. One spelling term_codec is the canonical form both the loader and the binder use. IRI: <http://example.edu/univ#Alice> Plain literal: "Alice" Language-tagged: "Alice"@en Datatype: "22"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> Blank node: _:b0 Escapes are part of the spelling. Two sources that mean the same IRI must intern once. Insert of an existing spelling returns the original id. Numeric datatypes ( xsd:integer , xsd:decimal , xsd:double , xsd:float ) compare by value in filters and in ORDER BY . Everything else compares by id for equality, and by the canonical spelling for ordered comparisons of the same kind. Memory dictionary MemDictionary is a mutex-guarded map in both directions. It is what the shell uses today. The mutex lets two sessions share the process. It is not isolation. Locks come later. Status Loading data/tiny.ttl interns every term and stores 53 triples in MemStore . Lookups used to print a result go through this dictionary. Nothing is written to a file. Term heap On disk, the bytes of a spelling live in a slotted page, not in the B+ tree leaf. A leaf key is three ids, 24 bytes, so the fanout stays high. A leaf that stored the IRIs would be a leaf of strings, and a split would copy those strings. TermHeap::Insert returns nullopt when the record does not fit on the page you asked. A record larger than an empty page throws StorageException . Get is valid only while the page is pinned. Delete frees the slot. A later insert may reuse it. FreeSpace includes the slot-directory entry, so the test captures free space before the delete and does not compare the page to itself. The heap chains pages. Its iterator visits every live record once and holds no pin after operator* returns. The page layout is in term_heap_page.h : after the pageLSN, the next page id, the slot count, and the start of the record area, then 4-byte slots (offset and length). Records grow down from the end of the page. Delete compacts the page at once, sliding the records below the deleted one up, so free space is always one gap and slot numbers never change. A record is at most 4,076 bytes; a longer term throws StorageException . An insert goes to the last page of the chain and chains a new page when it does not fit; space freed on earlier pages is not hunted for, because the dictionary never deletes terms. Disk dictionary Both directions survive restart: spelling to id, and id to spelling. Ids stay dense from 1. Call CheckAssignable before handing out a new id. Do not intern a spelling twice after restart, or one IRI becomes two ids and every join on that IRI breaks. OntoDB builds the dictionary from its own parts. Spellings live in a term heap. A B+ tree keyed (id, heap page, heap slot) answers id to spelling with a 1-prefix scan. A B+ tree keyed (hash, id, 0) answers spelling to id: a 1-prefix scan on the spelling's hash lists candidate ids, and each candidate's spelling is read and compared, so two spellings with the same hash are both found correctly. The hash is 64-bit FNV-1a, written out in the code, because a hash stored on disk must be the same in every build; std::hash is not. A header page, which the catalog's dictionary root names, holds the magic ODIC , the term count, and the three page ids. One mutex serializes the dictionary. A lookup by spelling costs two tree descents and a heap read; nothing is rebuilt at startup. The catalog remembers the dictionary root next to the permutation roots. Flush makes that metadata durable. Planned Plans 3.1 (term heap), 3.2 (disk dictionary), and 3.3 (c

title: Disk persistence design
text: Three words get borrowed from log-structured stores and do not name three background jobs here. Persistence is a snapshot plus the log today, and the database file plus the log once pages exist. Space comes back when a delete merges or reuses a slot. On the page path, a snapshot is a copied scan result or a lock held until commit. The persistent databases that run today keep a different, simpler pair of files; see Persistent databases . Persistence Two files, once the disk path exists. This is the page path, plans 1.1, 3.6, and 8.3 to 8.7. The database file is a sequence of 4096-byte pages. DiskManager owns it. Page ids survive restart. Each page image starts with an 8-byte pageLSN. The catalog, page 0, records the header page of spo , pos , and osp , and the dictionary's root. Term spellings live in the term heap, which is more pages in that same file. Triple keys live in the B+ tree leaves. The log is a separate append-only file. LogManager is constructed with a log_path . Append assigns an LSN. Flush makes every record up to that LSN durable. Commit forces the commit record. That commit record is the acknowledgement a later open will trust. Status The page path is being built. DiskManager::ShutDown (plan 1.1) fsyncs the file, and FlushAllPages (plan 1.4) writes every dirty frame; nothing calls them on the shell's path until the indexed store exists. CheckpointManager::Checkpoint throws plan 8.5. The in-memory database is durable through its own snapshot and log; see Persistent databases . A clean close and a crash are different successes. A clean close is plan 3.6. Flush every dirty frame, flush the catalog, then ShutDown the file. The next process reads the pages and does not need the log. An unflushed dirty frame is a lost triple even when nobody crashed. A crash is the recovery feature. The policy is steal / no-force, described in WAL and ARIES . An uncommitted page may already be on disk. A committed page may not be. Redo installs committed history the pages missed. Undo removes loser triples the pages kept. \crash exits without flushing, which is how you test that path on purpose. What becomes durable, and when: Event Durable after Insert still in a transaction the log record, only if a dirty page was stolen and the WAL rule flushed first \commit the commit record is on the log \checkpoint the checkpoint record, and whatever a blocking checkpoint also forced Process exit through ShutDown every dirty page and the catalog \crash only what a previous flush already wrote The shell knobs pool_size and lru_k change which pages stay in memory. They do not change the file format. Planned Plan 1.1 creates the database file. Plan 3.6 is the clean restart. Plans 8.1 through 8.7 are the log, the WAL rule, and crash recovery. Build the clean close before you depend on ARIES, so a shutdown bug is not mistaken for a recovery bug. Reclaiming space The index is one B+ tree per permutation. A key lives in exactly one leaf of that tree. A delete removes the key and then merges or redistributes so every node except the root stays at least half full. That work finishes inside BPlusTree::Remove , before the call returns. There is no later job that rewrites sorted runs. A missing key deletes nothing. A removed key does not stay behind as a marker for a reader to skip. Readers of a leaf see the keys that are still there. Crash recovery can still undo that delete, by the logical triple record and a CLR, if the transaction did not commit. The leaf after recovery contains the key again because undo put it back, not because a tombstone was compacted away. The term heap is looser. Delete on a heap page frees a slot, and a later insert may reuse it. FreeSpace counts that hole. Nothing in the plan rewrites a heap page to slide the survivors together, so a page can stay sparse when the hole is smaller than the next spelling. Deleting a triple does not drop the spelling. title: File formats
text: Write-ahead log ( wal ) The log is a sequence of records, each self-describing. Fields are in the machine's native byte order. u32 size whole record, header included u32 crc32c over every byte after this field u8 type i64 lsn log sequence number, from 1 i64 txn_id i64 prev_lsn previous record of the same transaction then, by type: update i32 page_id, u8 is_insert, u64 subject, u64 predicate, u64 object clr the update fields, then i64 undo_next checkpoint u32 n, then n x i64 active transaction ids term u64 term_id, u32 n, then n bytes of the canonical spelling begin, commit, abort: nothing more Type Written by a persistent database Meaning begin Yes A transaction starts term Yes A dictionary entry: id and spelling. Replayed in order so ids are identical after a restart update Yes One triple inserted or deleted, as three dictionary ids. page_id is -1 : the in-memory store has no pages commit Yes The transaction is durable abort, clr, checkpoint No Reserved for the page-based store's recovery The checksum is CRC-32C (Castagnoli), as in PostgreSQL, RocksDB, and InnoDB log records. A record that is cut short is a torn write; a record whose bytes are all present but whose checksum, type, or size is wrong is corruption. Both stop replay at that record; see Recovery on open . Snapshot ( snapshot ) A text file: a header, a blank line, then the body. ontodb-snapshot 1 lsn 37 txn 3 terms 18 triples 15 crc32c 1a2b3c4d T <http://example.org/materials#Material> T "Material" ... S 2 9 1 ... Line Meaning lsn The last log record the snapshot includes txn The next transaction id terms , triples Counts, checked on read crc32c Eight hex digits, over the whole body T<tab>spelling One dictionary term; the first is id 1, the next id 2, and so on S s p o One triple, as three term ids A snapshot is written to snapshot.tmp , synced, and renamed over snapshot . A wrong header, count, or checksum refuses to open.

title: Introduction
text: This manual describes how to install OntoDB, load ontologies, query and update them, keep a database on disk, and recover it after a crash. The last parts describe how OntoDB works inside and how the project is developed. For the theory behind each part (pages, buffer pools, B+ trees, query plans, locking, the write-ahead log, and ARIES), read the companion book, OntoDB: Database Internals by Example . Its design-decision boxes explain why OntoDB is built the way it is: each names the choice, the alternatives, and the cost. What OntoDB does today Loads Turtle, N-Triples, and RDF/XML. OWL files load as RDF triples; there is no reasoner. Answers SPARQL SELECT queries over a basic graph pattern with FILTER , and runs INSERT DATA and DELETE DATA . See SPARQL reference . Keeps a database on disk when started with a directory: every update is a transaction, a checksummed write-ahead log records it, \checkpoint writes a snapshot, and reopening the directory restores every committed transaction. See Persistent databases . Checks itself: \verify rebuilds the database from its files and compares it with the live one. Indexes, the cost-based optimizer, concurrent transactions, and the page-based disk store are designed and being built. See Roadmap . Quick start cmake --preset dev && cmake --build --preset dev ./build/dev/ontodb mydb OntoDB> \load data/tiny.owl loaded 14 triples in 5.2 ms OntoDB> SELECT ?kind WHERE { ?kind <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#subClassOf> <http://example.org/materials#Material> . } ?kind <http://example.org/materials#Metal> <http://example.org/materials#Polymer> (2 rows) Installation has the prerequisites, and the Tutorial walks through a full session. How this manual is organized Getting started Install, build, and a first session from load to recovery. Using OntoDB The shell, SPARQL, loading data, persistent databases, and settings. Reference On-disk file formats, messages, and troubleshooting. Internals Query engine, dictionary, indexes, B+ tree, buffer pool, concurrency, and recovery. Project Building and testing, the roadmap, and how results are reported. Conventions OntoDB> is the shell prompt. Commands that start with \ are shell commands; everything else is SPARQL. A Status box says what works today. A Planned box describes work that is designed but not built. Features that are not built yet answer not built yet (PLAN x.y) , where x.y is the item in the project's PLAN.md .

title: Triple indexes
text: TripleKey is 24 bytes: subject, predicate, object, each a big-endian uint64 . Order is memcmp on those bytes. sizeof(TripleKey) is 24. There is no padding to lean on. The 24-byte key Big-endian is what makes integer order and byte order the same. Little-endian would sort 256 before 1, and a prefix scan would be wrong even if Compare special-cased it. Encode(0x0102, 0, 0) stores 0x01 at byte 6 and 0x02 at byte 7. PrefixLower(key, n) is the smallest key whose first n components equal key 's. PrefixUpper(key, n) is the smallest key strictly above every key with that prefix. A scan of [lower, upper) is exactly the prefix. n is 0, 1, 2, or 3. For the key (5, 7, 9) : n Lower Upper 0 (0, 0, 0) past every key 1 (5, 0, 0) (6, 0, 0) 2 (5, 7, 0) (5, 8, 0) 3 (5, 7, 9) (5, 7, 10) n = 3 is a point lookup. n = 1 on SPO is "every triple with this subject". When nothing lies above the prefix, n = 0 or every bound id at the maximum, the upper bound saturates to the all- 0xFF key. That is three INVALID_TERM_ID s, which the dictionary never assigns, so the scan still covers every stored triple. A prefix length outside 0 to 3 throws std::invalid_argument . Planned Plan 0.2 is done. scripts/check 0.2 runs the round-trip, ordering, prefix-bound, carry, and saturation tests. The B+ tree is the key's first user. Permutations One order cannot serve every pattern. SPO answers a bound subject. It does not answer a bound object with an unbound subject, except by scanning the whole tree and filtering. The default store keeps three: "spo" , "pos" , and "osp" . Hexastore would build all six. RDF-3X argues you can stop earlier. OntoDB measured before choosing (plan 3.5): on LUBM(1), about 100,000 triples, with each pattern shape on a cold 64-frame pool, SPO alone reads all 1,131 pages for any pattern that binds the predicate or the object without the subject; POS and OSP cut that to 128 and 25 pages for twice the space (16 MiB against 8). The other three permutations cost 80% more space and made no pattern cheaper. benchmarks/indexing/results.md has the full table, and benchmarks/indexing/run.sh reruns it after scripts/fetch-data lubm . Pattern A prefix of subject bound SPO subject and predicate SPO predicate bound POS predicate and object POS object bound OSP object and subject OSP, or a filter on SPO if you accept the scan all bound any, as a point lookup nothing bound a full scan of any permutation All eight bound/unbound patterns must return the right triples even when only SPO exists. The extra permutations change the cost, not the answer. "All six" is the wrong default: each extra tree costs pages, and two or three cover the patterns that show up in real SPARQL. Indexed store Insert returns false if the triple is present. Delete returns false if it is absent. Either call updates every index the catalog has a root for, or it leaves the store unchanged. A scan returns IndexedTripleIterator , which drops its leaf guard when it dies. With only SPO, a pattern that is not a prefix of SPO is a scan plus a filter. \set backend indexed switches the shell to this store. The store names each permutation by its key order ( spo , pos , ...) and keeps whichever the catalog lists; a fresh catalog gets the default set. Insert and Delete reach every index or, if one throws, put the earlier ones back before the error propagates. Scan uses the index with the longest bound prefix and filters the other bound positions. In the shell, \set backend indexed builds a pool ( pool_size , lru_k ), the catalog, a disk dictionary, and the store in a temporary file, moves every triple across by spelling, and runs statements one at a time, because the tree is single-threaded until plan 7.1. \set backend mem moves the triples back and deletes the file. A persistent database ( ontodb <dir> ) stays on the memory backend until page-level recovery. The differential test builds a disk stack per query file. While DiskManager throws, the test skips and CI stays green. When the stack exists, it

Preset Build Use it for dev Debug with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer Everyday work tsan Debug with ThreadSanitizer Anything concurrent release Optimized Benchmarks Check the build ./build/dev/ontodb_test Every enabled test should pass. Tests for features that are not built yet are disabled and reported as such; see Development . Run ./build/dev/ontodb # an in-memory database that keeps nothing ./build/dev/ontodb mydb # a persistent database in the directory mydb ./build/dev/ontodb --strict mydb --strict refuses to open a database whose log is damaged, instead of recovering the valid part. Each feature's page in Internals describes its design. Feature Check Done when Optimizer scripts/check optimizer A rewritten plan returns the same rows Bulk load scripts/check load About 100k LUBM triples load under a small pool Concurrency scripts/check concurrency The feature is green under ThreadSanitizer Recovery scripts/check recovery scripts/crashtest --seeds 200 exits 0 Left open These have no stubs. Each starts as a design written next to its code, then a benchmark, then a writeup . Another eviction policy beside LRU-K. A different set of index permutations. MVCC beside strict two-phase locking. Restore to a chosen LSN: replay the snapshot and the log up to an LSN and stop. Planned The 24-byte key: scripts/check key . See Triple indexes .

title: Optimizer
text: A SPARQL join of four patterns has a factorial number of orders and three algorithms at each edge: nested loop, index nested loop, and hash join. The memory planner always picks the textual order and nested loop. That is a correct plan. It is not the plan you want on LUBM. Optimizer::Optimize takes that tree and returns another tree. The new tree must return the same rows. Config::join forces the algorithm when it is not kAuto : kNestedLoop stays a nested loop. kHash becomes a hash join. The plan text contains HashJoin . kIndexNestedLoop becomes an index nested-loop join. kAuto may pick any of the three. The factory already builds the executor from the node type. Slice 5.4 swaps the node. It does not teach the executor to ignore its own type. Status Optimize throws PLAN 5.3 . \explain analyze throws PLAN 5.5 . Statistics and the cardinality estimator throw their own plan ids. The shell setting \set join auto|nlj|inlj|hash is stored either way. Planned scripts/check optimizer covers slices 5.1 through 5.5, in that order. Join-method selection also depends on the executors from 4.2 and 4.3. You can collect statistics as soon as a store and a dictionary exist. Statistics Collect runs at load. Four numbers are the contract, and you may add more: TripleCount DistinctCount("s"|"p"|"o") PredicateCount , how many triples use a given predicate id PatternCount , how many triples match a partially bound pattern PatternCount may scan. It does not have to be clever. The estimator is what has to be cheap, because planning calls it on every alternative. OntoDB's Collect (plan 5.1, done) scans the store once and keeps counts per subject, predicate, and object, per pair of positions, and the set of triples. Every PatternCount is then an exact hash lookup, for every combination of bound positions; pair counts alone cannot answer a fully bound pattern, because all three pairs of a triple that is not stored can each occur elsewhere. That costs about seven hash entries per triple. The counts are a snapshot: updates after Collect leave them stale until the next collection. Cardinality Estimates are finite and never negative. A pattern with nothing bound estimates TripleCount . Binding one more position never increases the estimate. The usual formula treats positions as independent. Two bound positions estimate |p| * |o| / |T| . Check that against PatternCount on a few real patterns and write down the worst q-error, which is the ratio of estimate to truth, taking the worse direction. A fully unbound pattern joined with itself is not TripleCount for the join result. The second copy is correlated through the shared variables. An estimate that ignores the correlation will look precise and still pick a bad order. Join order Start greedy and left-deep. Enumerate bushy plans only after left-deep works. The test checks rows, not which order you picked. Your own timing experiment is what checks the order. Selinger's search keeps, for each subset of patterns, the cheapest way to produce it, plus interesting orders if you later add sort. OntoDB's first version can ignore interesting orders and keep one winner per subset. ORDER BY is an operator above the joins, not a reason to preserve a permutation's order, until you decide that a range scan is already sorted. Join method Cost the three algorithms with the cardinalities you just estimated. Nested loop is |outer| * |inner| in the worst pattern, and it needs no memory. Index nested loop is |outer| prefix probes. It wins when the inner pattern becomes a short range once the outer row is bound, which is the common SPARQL case: the outer row names a subject, and SPO is a point or a short range. Hash join is linear in the two inputs and needs memory for the build side. It loses when the build side is the whole store, when the key is almost unique so the index was already a point lookup, and when you cannot afford the table. Forcing kHash belongs in the optimizer because the executor must not secretly become a hash

title: Persistent databases
text: The directory mydb/ snapshot a full image of the database at one LSN (after the first \checkpoint) wal every log record after the snapshot Do not edit either file. Both carry checksums, and a change is reported as damage. Transactions Each update statement and each \load is one transaction. OntoDB applies it, writes its log records (begin, any new dictionary terms, one record per changed triple, commit), and forces the commit to disk before printing the result. When you see inserted 1 triple , the triple will be there after a crash. A statement that fails partway is undone, and nothing it changed is visible. A statement that changes nothing writes nothing to the log. Checkpoints \checkpoint writes a snapshot and empties the log: OntoDB> \checkpoint checkpoint at lsn 37: 18 terms, 15 triples; wal reset The snapshot is written to a temporary file, synced, and renamed over the old one, so a crash leaves either the old snapshot or the new one. If a crash comes after the rename but before the log is emptied, the next open skips every log record the snapshot already contains. Checkpoint when the log has grown, to make the next open faster. Recovery on open Opening a directory loads the snapshot, then replays the log after it. Only transactions with a commit record are applied; a transaction cut off by a crash leaves no trace. The first line says what happened: opened mydb: snapshot at lsn 61 (28 triples); wal 3 records, 1 committed, 0 uncommitted dropped; 27 triples If the log ends in a damaged record, there are two modes: Mode Start with At the first damaged record Point in time (default) ontodb mydb Keeps every transaction before it, cuts the log there, and prints a warning with the number of bytes discarded Absolute consistency ontodb --strict mydb Refuses to open A torn final record is what a crash usually leaves, and point in time is the right answer for it. Use --strict when any damage should stop you so you can inspect the files first. A damaged snapshot always refuses to open. Verify OntoDB> \verify snapshot: ok (lsn 37, 18 terms, 15 triples) wal: ok (0 records, 0 bytes) replay: matches the live database (15 triples) invariants: ok (no duplicate triples, every id in the dictionary) verify: ok \verify checks the snapshot and log checksums, rebuilds the database from the two files into a fresh store, compares it with the live database, and checks that no triple is stored twice and every id resolves in the dictionary. It changes nothing. A FAILED line names what is wrong. What is durable when Event Durable after An update or \load prints its result Its commit record is on disk A statement fails Nothing; it was undone \checkpoint returns The new snapshot, and an empty log \quit Everything committed \crash or a killed process Everything committed; anything else is lost Limits One process per directory. Two shells on the same directory are not supported. The whole database is held in memory; the directory is its durable copy. The page-based disk store, which does not need to fit in memory, is planned (see Roadmap ). The file layouts are in File formats .

title: Query engine
text: The planner does not run the query. It builds a tree. The execution engine asks a factory for the matching executor tree and pulls rows until Next returns false. Projection Filter age > 21 NestedLoopJoin TripleScan ?s a ub:Student TripleScan ?s ub:name ?name TripleScan ?s ub:age ?age Patterns join left to right. The filter sits above the joins. ORDER BY sits under the projection when it is present. Projection, then distinct, then limit. INSERT DATA and DELETE DATA plan to one insert or delete node, which runs as ModifyExecutor (plan 4.6): it writes each triple to the store, which writes every index or none, and returns the number changed as its one row. If a later write throws, it takes back the triples the statement already changed, so a statement is atomic on both backends even without a log. Triple scan TripleScanExecutor calls TripleStore::Scan(pattern) and gets a TripleIterator . Bound positions must match. If the same variable occurs twice inside one pattern, the scan keeps a triple only when those positions are equal. An empty pattern is one empty row, not zero rows. That is the identity input for a join that has nothing to bind yet. Status The scan runs against MemStore . The iterator is a snapshot of the matching triples. Destroying it does not unpin anything, because the memory store has no pages. Nested-loop join The join merges two rows by slot. Where both sides have a real id, the ids must be equal. Where one side is unbound, the other's id wins. The output width is the query's slot count, not the sum of the two children. The current join full-scans the inner child for every outer row. It does not push the outer binding into the inner pattern. The result is still correct, because the merge rejects pairs whose shared slots disagree. The cost is a full inner scan even when the outer row has already named the subject. Planned Plan 4.1, done: the nested loop reopens its inner side with InitWith(outer row) . Every executor has InitWith , which by default is Init ; the triple scan overrides it and turns each variable the outer row binds into a constant in the pattern it hands the store. On the indexed backend that pattern is usually a subject prefix, so each inner scan is a short range instead of a scan of every triple with that predicate. The test watches the pattern passed to Scan , not the output rows, because the rows were already right. Files: triple_scan_executor.cpp and nested_loop_join_executor.cpp . Plan 4.2, done: the index nested-loop join. Its inner side must be one triple pattern, and it has no inner executor: for each outer row it fills the pattern from that row and asks the store, which picks the index whose order starts with the bound positions. With rebinding the nested loop reads the same triples; the separate operator skips the inner executor and the generic merge, and names the strategy in the plan. \set join inlj selects it; a join whose inner side is not a scan stays a nested loop. On the memory backend the probe is a filtered scan. Plan 4.3, done: hash join. It reads the inner (right) side once into a table keyed by the ids of the variables both sides produce, then streams the outer side through it. A row whose key slot is unbound is not hashed; it is compared with every row of the other side. With no shared variable the key is empty and the join is a cross product. Building on the inner side is a stand-in until the optimizer can pick the smaller side. \set join hash selects it. \set join is applied by Optimizer::ApplyJoinMethod , which swaps the plan's join nodes before the plan is explained or run, so \explain shows the operator that runs. The differential test runs every query file under all three joins. Filter Equality and inequality are numeric when both sides are numeric datatypes, and term-id identity otherwise. Ordered comparisons are numeric, or lexicographic on the canonical spelling when the kinds match. A type error is false, not an exception. The query continues. Projection, distinct,

title: WAL and ARIES
text: The policy is steal / no-force. Steal means a dirty page of an uncommitted transaction may be written. No-force means a committed transaction's pages need not be written yet. Commit only has to make the commit record durable. Both choices are why a log exists: steal requires undo, no-force requires redo. The WAL rule A page is written only after every log record that describes that page image is durable. In the buffer pool that is a concrete order: The update sets the page's pageLSN to the LSN of its log record. FlushPage flushes the log up to that pageLSN. The crash point BufferPoolManager::FlushPage::before_disk_write may fire. The page is written. \crash exits without flushing. Anything not forced dies with the process. The commit record is the acknowledgement the crash harness trusts. An insert is visible after restart only if that commit reached disk. Planned Plan 8.3, after the log manager can flush. The test expects the new bytes to be absent from the file when the crash point fires. Run scripts/crashtest once with the log flush commented out, read the failure, and put the flush back. Log records Plan 8.1, done. SerializeTo writes Size() bytes. Deserialize reads one record. Size() on the deserialized record equals the number of bytes consumed. Every record starts with its length and a CRC-32C, the checksum PostgreSQL, RocksDB, and InnoDB put on their log records. The checksum covers every byte after it. u32 size whole record, header included u32 crc32c over every byte after this field u8 type i64 lsn, i64 txn_id, i64 prev_lsn then, by type, the fields below Type What it carries begin, commit, abort the transaction id update page id, whether this update inserted, and the triple CLR the update fields, and undo_next checkpoint the active transactions term a dictionary id and its canonical spelling The term record is for the memory database: replaying term records into an empty dictionary rebuilds the same ids. Two failures are kept apart. A buffer shorter than the record throws StorageException ; that is a torn final write, the expected shape of a crash. A record whose bytes are all there but wrong, with a bad checksum, a bad type, or an impossible size, throws LogCorruptionException . prev_lsn chains the records of one transaction, newest toward the begin record. Log manager An in-memory buffer and a background flush thread. Append assigns an LSN and returns it. Flush(lsn) blocks until every record up to that LSN is durable. Commit calls Flush with force. StartFlushThread starts the thread. StopFlushThread flushes the rest and joins. Each physical flush counts LogFlush when stats are installed. \log prints DebugTail , the last n records, oldest first. Group commit: commits that arrive while a flush is running share that flush, so GetFlushCount grows slower than the number of commits. A single client pays the latency of its own flush. A crowd of clients pays one flush per batch. If every commit flushes alone, the group-commit test fails. Plan 8.2, done. Opening a log that already has records continues its LSNs after the last valid one. LSNs start at 1. Without a running flush thread, Flush writes on the caller's thread. The destructor flushes; \crash exits without destructors, so whatever is buffered is lost. Torn and corrupt records ScanLog returns the valid prefix of a log file and says where and why it stopped. What to do at that point is a policy, named after RocksDB's WAL recovery modes: Mode Shell What happens at the first bad record point in time ontodb <dir> Keep every transaction before it, truncate the log there, and print what was dropped absolute consistency ontodb --strict <dir> Refuse to open Point in time is also what a torn final write needs, so it is the default. A transaction whose commit record is past the bad record is not committed, which is the same answer a crash gives. \verify is the offline check, in the spirit of PostgreSQL's pg_amcheck , MySQL's CHECK TABLE , and RocksDB's VerifyChecksum . It rea

title: Benchmarks and writeups
text: The store stays one codebase. Eviction, which permutations exist, which join runs, and how often a checkpoint is taken are switches. Record the switch in the result table. Do not fork the repository to try a method. A comparison waits until the feature it measures exists. The directory is created then, not before. A question benchmarks/<question>/ question.md what is compared, on which data, and which metric decides run.sh the commands, with the dataset and the knobs results.md the table a writeup will cite raw/ logs and traces; this directory is not committed Directory Question Waits on eviction How do pool size and LRU-K change the hit ratio on one query mix? Buffer pool indexing Which permutations pay for themselves on LUBM? Triple indexes , bulk load joins Nested loop, index nested loop, hash, and the optimizer's own choice Query engine , optimizer recovery Group commit and checkpoint interval against throughput and restart time WAL and ARIES scripts/fetch-data lubm builds the LUBM(1) file for the indexing and join questions. It needs Java. data/tiny.ttl is the smoke graph, 53 triples, not a benchmark. question.md names the metric before the run. Hit ratio, pages read, load time, commit latency, and restart time are the ones these four questions can answer. A second metric can sit in the same table. It does not replace the one that decides. run.sh prints the knob values it used. A result with no knob is not comparable to the next run. A writeup A writeup is one file in writeups/ , written after results.md exists. The first paragraph states the method, the data, and the metric. It links the result table. Figures may be drawn from raw/ . The logs stay there and are not pasted into the writeup. The shape that stays readable later: The question, in one sentence. The methods, including the knob values. The data set and the query mix. The table from results.md . What the table does not show. A hit-ratio win with a slower load is still a result. Write it down. There is nothing to write up yet. The memory shell is the baseline those tables will be compared with, once the indexed store and the log exist. The query window The shell is the interface. A later window, desktop or local page, sends the same text and prints the same rows. It does not get a second parser, a second planner, or its own notion of a result. Benchmarks keep using the shell and run.sh , so a UI change cannot move a number. Status benchmarks/README.md and writeups/README.md are the contract. No question directory has a results.md yet. Planned The next code is still the triple key . The first comparison that can be run after that is eviction, and only once the buffer pool reports hits and misses.

title: Shell reference
text: Starting the shell ontodb [--strict] [--db] [dir] Invocation Database ontodb In memory. Nothing is kept after \quit ontodb dir or ontodb --db dir Persistent, in dir , created if missing. The first line reports what was recovered ontodb --strict dir Persistent, but refuses to open if the log is damaged The shell reads standard input, so a script can be piped in: ontodb mydb < script.txt . The prompt OntoDB> is printed before each statement whenever the shell reads standard input, piped or not; with sessions it shows the session number, OntoDB:2> . How input is read A line that starts with \ is one shell command. Anything else is SPARQL. A statement may span lines and runs when its { } group has opened and closed and every string is closed. A PREFIX line stays pending until the query that uses it is complete. # starts a comment, except inside a string or an IRI, so <http://example.edu/univ#Student> is read whole. \quit leaves at once, even in the middle of a statement. Commands Command What it does \load path Loads a Turtle ( .ttl ), N-Triples ( .nt ), or RDF/XML ( .rdf , .owl ) file. In a persistent database the whole file is one transaction SPARQL statement Runs a query or an update. In a persistent database an update is one transaction \explain query Prints the plan without running it \explain analyze query Not built (PLAN 5.5) \checkpoint Persistent databases: writes a snapshot and empties the log \verify Persistent databases: checks the snapshot and log, rebuilds from them, and compares with the live database \log [n] Persistent databases: prints the last n log records (default 20), oldest first \crash Persistent databases: exits immediately without flushing, to test recovery \stats Prints page, buffer, and log counters \timing on or off Prints each statement's time after its result \set Prints the settings \set knob value Changes a setting. See Settings \session n Sends the following input to session n , creating it if needed \help Lists the commands \quit , \q Leaves the shell In an in-memory database, \checkpoint , \log , and \crash answer not built yet , and \verify says there is nothing on disk to verify. \bpm and \page <id> inspect the buffer pool; with the default memory backend they answer no buffer pool . \trace on|off prints component events to stderr. \tree spo and \tree spo dot draw an index on the indexed backend. These commands belong to features still being built and answer not built yet (PLAN x.y) : \begin , \commit , \abort , \txns , and \locks (transactions, 7.2 and 7.3). Results and errors A query prints its variables on one line, then one row per line in canonical spelling ( <iri> , "literal" , "lex"@en , "lex"^^<datatype> , _:blank ), then a row count. An update prints how many triples it changed: inserted 1 triple , deleted 0 triples . A statement never crashes the shell. A parse or bind error prints its line and column; any other failure prints error: and a message. See Messages and troubleshooting . Sessions \quit , \help , and \session run on the main thread. Every other command runs on the current session's worker thread. Sessions share one database. Until transactions are built, sessions are separate prompts, not isolated transactions.

title: SPARQL reference
text: Queries PREFIX ub: <http://example.edu/univ#> SELECT ?name WHERE { ?s a ub:Student ; ub:name ?name ; ub:age ?age . FILTER (?age > 21 && ?age <= 30) } Feature Supported PREFIX declarations Yes SELECT ?a ?b and SELECT * Yes. * projects every variable in order of first appearance Basic graph pattern, one group Yes. a means rdf:type ; ; repeats the subject; , repeats subject and predicate FILTER with = != < > <= >= combined by && Yes DISTINCT , LIMIT , OFFSET , ORDER BY Parsed and shown by \explain ; running them answers not built yet (PLAN 4.4, 4.5) OPTIONAL , UNION , nested groups, property paths, aggregates Rejected Numbers in a query are xsd:integer or xsd:decimal literals and compare numerically with numeric literals in the data. Updates INSERT DATA { <http://ex/a> <http://ex/p> "one" . } DELETE DATA { <http://ex/a> <http://ex/p> "one" . } Only ground triples: no variables, no WHERE . Inserting a triple that is already stored, or deleting one that is not, changes nothing and is not an error. DELETE/INSERT WHERE is rejected. In a persistent database each update statement is one transaction. Terms Every term has one canonical spelling, shared by the loader, the query, and the results: Term Spelling IRI <http://example.org/materials#Metal> Plain literal "Metal" Language-tagged literal "Métal"@fr Typed literal "21"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> Blank node _:b0 Rejected features OPTIONAL , UNION , property paths, aggregates, and DELETE/INSERT WHERE fail with the feature's name, a line, and a column: OntoDB> SELECT ?x WHERE { ?x ?p ?o . OPTIONAL { ?x ?q ?r } } error: OPTIONAL is not supported at line 1, column 30 No reasoning OWL loads as RDF triples. rdfs:subClassOf is data, not a rule, so a query for instances of a class does not return instances of its subclasses. For LUBM, queries 4, 5, 6, and 11 to 13 return a subset for this reason. Further reading SPARQL 1.1 Query Language (W3C), the sections on basic graph patterns, FILTER , and INSERT DATA / DELETE DATA .

Any other failure. The statement changed nothing Read the message When opening a directory Message Meaning What to do opened dir: ... Everything before it was kept Run \verify . If damage was not expected, check the disk error: wal: ... not opening in absolute-consistency mode --strict found a damaged log record Copy the directory, then open without --strict to recover the valid part error: snapshot: checksum mismatch (or a bad header or count) The snapshot file was changed or damaged Restore it from a copy. A damaged snapshot cannot be recovered automatically error: wal: lsn N gives term T a different spelling The log disagrees with the snapshot about a dictionary id The files come from different databases, or one was edited Questions A query for a class does not return instances of its subclasses. OntoDB does not reason; subClassOf is data. See No reasoning . A load is slow on a large file. The in-memory store is not indexed. See Loading data . The log keeps growing. Run \checkpoint .

title: Tutorial
text: Create a database and load an ontology Start the shell with a directory. OntoDB creates it if it does not exist. $ ./build/dev/ontodb mydb opened mydb: no snapshot; wal 0 records, 0 committed, 0 uncommitted dropped; 0 triples OntoDB> \load data/tiny.owl loaded 14 triples in 5.2 ms data/tiny.owl is an OWL ontology in RDF/XML with four classes: Material, Metal, Alloy, and Polymer. The load is one transaction. When the line loaded 14 triples appears, those triples are on disk. Query A query may span lines. It runs when its braces close. OntoDB> PREFIX m: <http://example.org/materials#> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> SELECT ?kind WHERE { ?kind rdfs:subClassOf m:Material . } ?kind <http://example.org/materials#Metal> <http://example.org/materials#Polymer> (2 rows) Alloy is not listed: it is a subclass of Metal, and OntoDB stores subClassOf as data, not as a rule to reason with. Update OntoDB> INSERT DATA { <http://example.org/materials#Ceramic> <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#subClassOf> <http://example.org/materials#Material> . } inserted 1 triple OntoDB> \log 3 lsn 35 txn 2 term 18 <http://example.org/materials#Ceramic> lsn 36 txn 2 update insert (18 9 4) lsn 37 txn 2 commit OntoDB> \quit \log shows the transaction the insert wrote: a dictionary entry for the new IRI, the triple as three ids, and the commit. Reopen $ ./build/dev/ontodb mydb opened mydb: no snapshot; wal 37 records, 2 committed, 0 uncommitted dropped; 15 triples OntoDB> SELECT ?kind WHERE { ?kind <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#subClassOf> <http://example.org/materials#Material> . } ?kind <http://example.org/materials#Metal> <http://example.org/materials#Polymer> <http://example.org/materials#Ceramic> (3 rows) The open replayed the two committed transactions, the load and the insert. Checkpoint and verify OntoDB> \checkpoint checkpoint at lsn 37: 18 terms, 15 triples; wal reset OntoDB> \verify snapshot: ok (lsn 37, 18 terms, 15 triples) wal: ok (0 records, 0 bytes) replay: matches the live database (15 triples) invariants: ok (no duplicate triples, every id in the dictionary) verify: ok The checkpoint wrote a snapshot and emptied the log, so the next open loads the snapshot instead of replaying every record. \verify read both files back, rebuilt the database from them, and found it identical to the one in memory.
